column1: Azure Event Hub Namespace having authorization rules except RootManageSharedAccessKey
column3:
This policy identifies Azure Event Hub Namespaces which have authorization rules except RootManageSharedAccessKey.

Having Azure Event Hub namespace authorization rules other than 'RootManageSharedAccessKey' could provide access to all queues and topics under the namespace which pose a risk if these additional rules are not properly managed or secured.

As best practice, it is recommended to remove Event Hub namespace authorization rules other than RootManageSharedAccessKey and create access policies at the entity level, which provide access to only that specific entity for queues and topics.

column1: Internal NPM package is not scoped in GitLab repository
column3: Any third party can publish unscoped packages to the public NPM registry. If the organization does not own the names of the internal packages on the public registry, attackers could potentially upload malicious packages to the registry with identical or similar names, hoping that clients who have not configured their `.npmrc` files to fetch packages from the internal registry will mistakenly download them. Scoping packages in NPM can help protect against \"Dependency Confusion\" and Typosquatting attacks. This is because each NPM user/organization has their own scope, and only the user/organization`s owner can add packages to that scope. As a result, third parties cannot take the package name. Note: The package source displayed in the event field can be specified using one of the following methods described in these examples: • URL: https://registry.npmjs.org/example/-/example-1.0.0.tgz • Git URL: git+ssh://git@github.com/org/repo.git • Local file path: file:../foo/bar • Local linked package: folder/package

column1: Remote code execution (RCE) exploitation attempt on GCP VM with known exploitable vulnerability [Log4j, CVE-2021-45046]
column3:
Unauthorized remote code execution attempts targeting Google Cloud Platform (GCP) virtual machines (VMs) with the known Log4j vulnerability (CVE-2021-45046) pose a significant security risk. Attackers could leverage this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and control over the affected VMs. Successful exploitation allows arbitrary code execution, potentially leading to data breaches, system compromise, and disruption of services.

Exploitation typically involves sending a specially crafted network request exploiting the Log4j vulnerability. Successful exploitation grants the attacker complete control over the compromised VM, enabling data exfiltration, lateral movement within the cloud environment, and the installation of malware for persistent access. This compromises confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the affected resources and potentially sensitive data.

Mitigation involves immediately patching the vulnerable Log4j instances on all affected GCP VMs to the latest version. This is crucial to eliminate the vulnerability and prevent further exploitation attempts. Regular vulnerability scanning and patching processes are paramount for proactive security posture management. Implementing robust logging and monitoring for unusual network activity also helps detect potential exploitation attempts early.

To prevent future exploitation, promptly patch all vulnerable systems. Enable Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules to block known exploit attempts. Implement strong access controls, including least privilege, and regularly audit system configurations for security misconfigurations. Proactive vulnerability management is key to minimizing risk.

column1: Potentially unauthorized DNS rebinding activity detected on a publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instance
column3:
Publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instances with detected DNS rebinding activity pose a significant security risk. Attackers could exploit this attack path to compromise confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

DNS rebinding attacks leverage the ephemeral nature of DNS records to bypass security controls. Attackers might exploit vulnerabilities on a publicly accessible EC2 instance, using it as a proxy to access internal resources like the AWS Metadata Service. This allows access to sensitive data, including temporary AWS credentials, leading to further compromise.

Mitigate this risk by immediately patching identified vulnerabilities on the EC2 instance. Restrict public access to the EC2 instance by configuring appropriate security groups and network ACLs. Regular vulnerability scanning and penetration testing are crucial preventative measures.

To break the attack chain, promptly address the identified vulnerabilities and restrict public access. Implement robust network segmentation and regularly review and update security configurations. Employ web application firewalls (WAFs) to further mitigate DNS rebinding attempts.

This policy identifies an AWS IAM user as not being a member of any IAM group.

It is generally a best practice to assign IAM users to at least one IAM group. If the IAM users are not in a group, it complicates permission management and auditing, increasing the risk of privilege mismanagement and security oversights. It also leads to higher operational overhead and potential non-compliance with security best practices.

It is recommended to ensure all IAM users are part of at least one IAM group according to your business requirement to simplify permission management, enforce consistent security policies, and reduce the risk of privilege mismanagement.

This feature is useful for ensuring the security, integrity, and reliability of container images in production environments. It prevents tags from being overwritten, which can help prevent unauthorised changes to images.

It is recommended to enable tag immutability on ECR repositories to maintain the integrity and security of the images pushed.

column1: GCP VM instance with Shielded VM features disabled
column3:
This policy identifies VM instances which have Shielded VM features disabled. Shielded VMs are virtual machines (VMs) on Google Cloud Platform hardened by a set of security controls that help defend against rootkits and bootkits. Shielded VM's verifiable integrity is achieved through the use of Secure Boot, virtual trusted platform module (vTPM)-enabled Measured Boot, and integrity monitoring. Shielded VM instances run firmware which is signed and verified using Google's Certificate Authority, ensuring that the instance's firmware is unmodified and establishing the root of trust for Secure Boot.

NOTE: You can only enable Shielded VM options on instances that have Shielded VM support. This policy reports VM instances that have Shielded VM support and are disabled with the Shielded VM features.

column1: Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploitation attempt on Azure Virtual Machine with known exploitable vulnerability [Drupalgeddon2, CVE-2018-7600]
column3:
Unauthorized remote code execution attempts targeting Azure Virtual Machines with the known Drupalgeddon2 (CVE-2018-7600) vulnerability pose a significant security risk. Attackers could leverage this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and control of the affected machines. Successful exploitation allows for arbitrary code execution, data exfiltration, and further lateral movement within the environment.

Exploitation typically involves sending malicious requests exploiting the vulnerability in Drupal. Successful exploitation grants attackers complete control over the compromised virtual machine. This compromised machine can then be used as a launching point for attacks against other systems within the network, resulting in data breaches, service disruption, and reputational damage.

Mitigate this risk by immediately patching the vulnerable Drupal installation to the latest version. This is crucial to eliminate the vulnerability's exploitable surface. Regularly update all software components on your Azure VMs to prevent similar vulnerabilities from being exploited. Implement robust vulnerability scanning and patching processes to identify and remediate vulnerabilities promptly.

To prevent future occurrences, enforce a strict patching policy for all software components. Implement strong network security controls, such as firewalls and intrusion detection/prevention systems. Regularly conduct security assessments and penetration testing to identify and address vulnerabilities before they can be exploited.

column1: Remote command execution risk due to publicly exposed admin ports on Azure Virtual Machine with Run command permissions
column3:
Publicly exposed Azure Virtual Machines with 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommands/write' and 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommand/action' permissions enable remote command execution.

Attackers could exploit this attack path by accessing open admin ports (SSH/RDP) and leveraging these permissions to execute arbitrary commands on the Virtual Machine. This compromises the Virtual Machine and potentially allows lateral movement within the cloud environment, leading to data breaches or further compromise.

Mitigate this risk by immediately restricting public access to admin ports using network security groups (NSGs). Prioritize least privilege; remove unnecessary 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommands/write' and 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommand/action' permissions unless explicitly required for legitimate administrative tasks.

To avoid this, promptly review and revoke unnecessary 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommands/write' and 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommand/action' permissions. Implement NSGs to restrict inbound traffic to admin ports, allowing only trusted IP addresses or virtual networks.

column1: Azure MySQL (PaaS) instance with network path from the untrust internet source on TCP port 3306
column3:
Azure MySQL (PaaS) instances accessible from untrusted internet sources via TCP port 3306 pose a significant security risk. Public exposure of this port allows unauthorized access attempts, potentially leading to data breaches.

The Azure MySQL service's network configuration allows inbound connections on specific ports. Leaving port 3306 open to the internet without proper access controls creates a direct path for malicious actors to attempt unauthorized access using brute-force attacks or exploiting known vulnerabilities in the database or application. Successful compromise could lead to data exfiltration, modification, or deletion.

A misconfiguration exposing port 3306 publicly impacts data confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Restricting access to only trusted IP addresses minimizes the attack surface, limiting the potential for unauthorized access and mitigating the risk of data breaches. This best practice ensures that only authorized entities can connect to the database.

Mitigate this risk by configuring network security groups (NSGs) to allow inbound connections on port 3306 only from explicitly trusted IP addresses or virtual networks. Regularly review and update the allowed IP list to ensure it reflects current security needs. Consider implementing additional security measures such as strong passwords, multi-factor authentication, and database auditing.

column1: Remote code execution risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable Azure Virtual Machine (Apache ActiveMQ, CVE-2023-46604)
column3:
Publicly exposed Azure Virtual Machines running vulnerable Apache ActiveMQ (CVE-2023-46604) pose a significant remote code execution risk. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and control of the affected system.

Exploitation happens when an attacker leverages the CVE-2023-46604 flaw in ActiveMQ to execute malicious code. A publicly accessible VM increases the attack surface, making it easier for threat actors to compromise the machine and potentially access sensitive data or move laterally within the network. This leads to data breaches, service disruptions, and reputational damage.

Mitigation involves immediately patching the Apache ActiveMQ application to address CVE-2023-46604. Restricting network access to the VM, ensuring only authorized traffic can reach it, is crucial. Regular vulnerability scanning and patching are essential best practices.

To avoid future occurrences, enforce least privilege access, regularly update software, and implement robust network security controls like firewalls and intrusion detection systems. Prioritize patching vulnerable applications and promptly remediate security findings.

column1: Privilege escalation risk due to publicly exposed GCP VM instance with high/critical severity vulnerabilities assigned with high privilege role inactive for 90 days
column3:
This policy identifies publicly exposed GCP VM instances with high or critical severity vulnerabilities that have been assigned high-privilege roles and have been inactive for the past 90 days.

Publicly exposed VM instances with high or critical vulnerabilities pose a significant risk, as they can provide malicious actors with an entry point into the environment. When such instances are also assigned high-privilege roles, the risk escalates due to the extensive permissions granted. If the roles or permissions have not been utilized in the last 90 days, it strongly indicates they are unnecessary for the attached resources. Removing these permissions reduces the potential impact of a security breach.

Immediate action is required to mitigate these risks, including restricting public exposure of the identified VM instances, remediating high and critical vulnerabilities reported for the instances, and enforcing least privilege principles by removing redundant role assignments and permissions from the VM instances.

column1: Credential exposure risk due to a publicly exposed and vulnerable EC2 instance with risky credentials exposure permissions
column3:
Publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instances with excessive permissions pose a significant security risk. Malicious actors could compromise these instances, gaining unauthorized access to sensitive data and resources.

Attackers could exploit this attack path by leveraging publicly accessible vulnerabilities to gain initial access to the EC2 instance. The presence of excessive permissions, such as 'ec2:getpassworddata' and 'iam:createaccesskey', then allows attackers to escalate privileges and access other AWS resources, potentially leading to data breaches or account compromise.

Mitigation involves immediately restricting public access to the EC2 instance. This is crucial to prevent unauthorized access attempts. Next, review and minimize the instance's permissions, granting only the least privilege necessary for its intended function. Regular vulnerability scanning and patching are also essential for preventing exploitation.

To prevent future occurrences, enforce a least privilege security model. Regularly review and audit EC2 instance permissions, removing unnecessary access rights. Implement robust vulnerability management practices, including regular patching and automated scanning. Restrict public access to EC2 instances whenever possible.

It is recommended to use HTTPS protocol with external-facing load balancers.

column1: GCP Cloud Function has risky basic role assigned
column3:
Cloud Functions assigned overly permissive 'basic' roles pose a significant security risk. These roles grant extensive project access, increasing the impact of a compromise.

GCP Cloud Functions utilize IAM roles to control access. 'Basic' roles, unlike more granular roles introduced later, provide broad permissions. An attacker gaining control of a Cloud Function with a 'basic' role could potentially access and modify all project resources, leading to data breaches or service disruptions.

Exploiting this misconfiguration could result in complete project compromise, data exfiltration, unauthorized resource modification, or even complete service disruption. Using least privilege, by assigning only necessary permissions, significantly reduces the attack surface and limits the damage from a potential compromise.

Remediate this by replacing 'basic' roles with custom roles granting only the necessary roles for the Cloud Function. Regularly review assigned roles to ensure continued adherence to the principle of least privilege. This mitigates risk by limiting potential damage from a compromised Cloud Function.

column1: Privilege escalation risk due to Code/Command injection payload detected on traffic targetting a vulnerable Azure Virtual Machine with privilege escalation permissions
column3:
Code injection attacks targeting Azure Virtual Machines with excessive permissions pose a significant security risk. Successful exploitation allows attackers to execute arbitrary code, potentially leading to complete system compromise and data exfiltration.

Attackers might leverage vulnerabilities in web applications or services running on the VM to inject malicious code via various vectors, such as HTTP requests or input fields. Successful injection with elevated permissions ('Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory/b2cDirectories/write', 'Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities/write', etc.) grants extensive control, enabling data breaches, lateral movement, and persistent access.

Mitigate this risk by regularly patching applications and operating systems. Implement robust input validation and encoding to prevent code injection. Review and minimize the permissions assigned to VMs, granting only necessary privileges adhering to the principle of least privilege.

Immediately investigate suspicious network traffic targeting the vulnerable VM. Remove unnecessary permissions. Implement strong web application firewalls and intrusion detection systems to detect and block malicious code injection attempts.

column1: Remote code execution (RCE) risk due to a publicly exposed (via resource based policies) AWS Lambda Function with Spring4Shell vulnerability
column3:
Publicly accessible AWS Lambda functions with the Spring4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2022-22965 and CVE-2022-22963) pose a significant remote code execution (RCE) risk. Exploitation could lead to complete system compromise.

Attackers could leverage the publicly exposed Lambda function's Spring4Shell vulnerability to execute arbitrary code. This allows them to gain unauthorized access, steal data, or disrupt operations, resulting in significant data breaches and service disruptions.

Mitigation involves restricting access to the Lambda function. Employ least privilege principle by using resource-based policies to limit 'lambda:InvokeFunction' permission to only trusted entities or services. Regularly patch the Lambda function's runtime environment to address known vulnerabilities.

Immediately revoke 'lambda:InvokeFunction' permission from any unnecessary principals. Implement robust access controls, and continuously monitor for suspicious activity. Prioritize patching the Spring4Shell vulnerability in the Lambda function's runtime.

column1: Azure AKS K8s service with network path from the internet (0.0.0.0/0) on ports 80/443
column3:
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) clusters exposing ports 80 and 443 to the internet (0.0.0.0/0) present a significant security risk. This misconfiguration exposes the cluster to a wide range of attacks.

AKS clusters, by default, should not be directly accessible from the internet. Opening ports 80 and 443 to 0.0.0.0/0 allows untrusted IPs to directly access the Kubernetes API server and potentially any exposed applications within the cluster. This greatly expands the attack surface, making the cluster vulnerable to unauthorized access, data breaches, and service disruptions.

The impact of this misconfiguration could be severe, leading to data exfiltration, application compromise, and potential ransomware attacks. Implementing proper network segmentation and access controls is critical to minimize this risk. Restricting access to only trusted IP addresses or using a reverse proxy with appropriate authentication and authorization mechanisms is essential.

To mitigate this risk, limit network access to the AKS cluster. Use Network Policies to control traffic within the cluster. Implement a reverse proxy like Nginx or HAProxy in front of the services to handle external traffic and enforce security policies, such as authentication and authorization. Only allow trusted IP addresses to access the cluster.

The Regular release channel upgrades every few weeks and is for production users who need features not yet offered in the Stable channel. These versions have passed internal validation, but don't have enough historical data to guarantee their stability. Known issues generally have known workarounds.

The Stable release channel upgrades every few months and is for production users who need stability above all else, and for whom frequent upgrades are too risky. These versions have passed internal validation and have been shown to be stable and reliable in production, based on the observed performance of those clusters.

column1: Privilege escalation risk due to a publicly exposed and vulnerable GCP VM instance with Resource Manager permissions

Mitigate this risk by immediately restricting public access to all VMs. Apply least privilege principles; only grant necessary permissions to VMs. Regularly scan for vulnerabilities and remediate them promptly.

Prioritize patching and vulnerability remediation. Regularly review and minimize the permissions assigned to all compute instances. Implement strong network security controls, including firewalls, to prevent unauthorized access.

column1: Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploitation attempt on AWS EC2 instance with known exploitable vulnerability [OpenLiteSpeed, Multiple CVEs]
column3:
AWS EC2 instances with vulnerable OpenLiteSpeed installations are susceptible to remote code execution (RCE) exploits. Attackers could exploit this attack path by leveraging known vulnerabilities in the OpenLiteSpeed software.

Exploitation attempts manifest as suspicious network traffic patterns and processes indicative of malicious code execution. Successful exploitation grants attackers complete control over the compromised EC2 instance, leading to data breaches, service disruptions, and further lateral movement within the environment.

Mitigation involves immediately updating OpenLiteSpeed to the latest patched version. This eliminates the known vulnerabilities exploited by attackers, preventing RCE and significantly reducing the attack surface. Prioritize patching based on CVE severity and exploit prevalence.

To prevent future exploitation, implement robust vulnerability management practices. Regularly scan for and remediate vulnerabilities, enforce least privilege access, and implement intrusion detection and prevention systems to detect and block malicious activity.

column1: Azure Storage account configured with Shared Key authorization
column3:
Azure Storage accounts using Shared Key authorization are vulnerable to unauthorized access. Shared Key authorization, including access via Shared Access Signatures (SAS) tokens, allows access for any entity possessing the key, increasing the risk of data breaches.

Failing to utilize Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) authentication instead of Shared Key exposes the storage account to attacks from malicious actors who obtain the shared key, potentially leading to data exfiltration, modification, or deletion.

Misconfiguration of storage account authorization can result in significant data loss, regulatory fines, and reputational damage. Using Azure AD authentication provides stronger security through identity and access management, minimizing the risk of compromised credentials.

Implement Azure AD authentication for all Azure Storage accounts. Revoke any existing Shared Keys and SAS tokens. Regularly audit access permissions and enforce the principle of least privilege. Consider using Managed Identities for applications accessing storage.

column1: Potential indication of data exfiltration activity through a publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instance with s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket permissions and not configured with Metadata Service v2 (IMDSv2)
column3:
Publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instances with 's3:GetObject' and 's3:ListBucket' permissions, lacking IMDSv2, indicate potential data exfiltration.

Attackers can exploit vulnerabilities on publicly accessible EC2 instances. These instances, with excessive S3 permissions and using IMDSv1, enable access to sensitive metadata including temporary credentials. This allows attackers to access and exfiltrate data from associated S3 buckets. High data transfer volume from such compromised instances strongly suggests malicious activity.

Mitigate by immediately restricting internet access to the EC2 instance. Enforce the principle of least privilege, granting only necessary permissions. Implement IMDSv2 to enhance security and prevent unauthorized metadata access. Regularly review and update security groups.

Immediately revoke unnecessary permissions, particularly 's3:GetObject' and 's3:ListBucket'. Configure IMDSv2 and restrict public access to EC2 instances. Conduct a thorough security assessment to identify and remediate vulnerabilities.

column1: Privilege Escalation risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable GCP VM instance [OpenSSL, CVE-2022-3786]
column3:
Publicly exposed Google Cloud Platform (GCP) virtual machine (VM) instances with the OpenSSL vulnerability 'CVE-2022-3786' pose a significant privilege escalation risk. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to gain unauthorized elevated privileges on the affected VM.

Attackers may leverage automated scanning tools to identify publicly accessible VMs with known vulnerabilities like 'CVE-2022-3786'. Successful exploitation grants attackers control, enabling data breaches, lateral movement within the GCP environment, and further compromise of sensitive resources.

Mitigation involves promptly patching the OpenSSL vulnerability on all affected VMs by updating to the latest version. This eliminates the direct exploitation path for 'CVE-2022-3786'. Furthermore, ensure all VMs are appropriately configured with network firewalls to restrict public access, allowing only necessary inbound connections.

Immediately patch the OpenSSL vulnerability using the available updates. Restrict public access to VMs by configuring appropriate network firewalls and access control lists. Regularly scan for vulnerabilities and promptly address any identified issues.

column1: Remote code execution risk due to publicly exposed AWS EC2 instance with regreSSHion vulnerability (OpenSSH, CVE-2024-6387)
column3:
Publicly accessible AWS EC2 instances with the regreSSHion vulnerability ('CVE-2024-6387') in OpenSSH pose a critical remote code execution risk.

Attackers can exploit the 'CVE-2024-6387' vulnerability in older OpenSSH versions on publicly exposed EC2 instances without authentication. This allows them to gain root access, potentially leading to system compromise, data breaches, and lateral movement within the environment. The public exposure significantly increases the attack surface and ease of exploitation.

Mitigation involves immediately patching vulnerable OpenSSH versions to 4.4p1 or later, or 9.8p1 and above. Restricting network access to the EC2 instance by configuring appropriate security group rules to only allow necessary traffic is crucial. This prevents unauthorized access and reduces the attack surface.

To prevent future occurrences, implement a robust patching strategy for all software, especially critical components like OpenSSH. Regularly scan for vulnerabilities and enforce least privilege access controls. Immediately update or replace vulnerable instances.

column1: Remote code execution risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable Azure Virtual Machine (Redis Servers in Debian Linux, CVE-2022-0543)
column3:
Publicly exposed Azure Virtual Machines running vulnerable Redis servers (Debian Linux, CVE-2022-0543) pose a significant remote code execution risk. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and control.

Exploitation involves attackers scanning for publicly accessible VMs with the vulnerable Redis server. Successful exploitation grants complete control, enabling data theft, privilege escalation, and lateral movement within the organization's infrastructure. This compromises confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Mitigate this risk by immediately patching the vulnerable Redis servers with the latest security updates. Ensure all network security groups correctly restrict inbound access to only authorized sources. Regular vulnerability scanning and penetration testing are crucial for proactive risk management.

To prevent future occurrences, implement robust network segmentation, regularly update all software, and enforce the principle of least privilege. Immediately revoke unnecessary public network access for the affected VMs and ensure strong access controls.

column1: GCP Dataproc Serverless Session is using default network
column3:
Dataproc Serverless sessions using the default network in GCP pose a significant security risk. This misconfiguration exposes resources to unintended network access and lacks essential security controls.

The default network in GCP provides broad, unrestricted access between all instances. This lack of network segmentation allows unauthorized communication between sensitive and non-sensitive workloads. An attacker exploiting a misconfigured application within one instance could easily pivot to other instances within the default network. This lack of isolation dramatically increases the attack surface and the potential for data breaches or system compromises.

The impact of this misconfiguration includes data breaches, unauthorized access to sensitive information, and compromised application integrity. Employing a custom VPC with appropriate firewall rules and network segmentation ensures that only authorized traffic can access resources. This practice enhances security posture and reduces the likelihood of successful attacks.

To mitigate this risk, use a custom Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network for Dataproc Serverless. Configure appropriate firewall rules to restrict inbound and outbound network traffic to only authorized sources and destinations. Implement network segmentation by creating subnets for different workloads, further limiting the impact of potential breaches.

column1: Privilege Escalation risk due to unauthenticated public access and insecure permissions in an Azure Function
column3:
Unauthenticated public access to Azure Functions with excessive permissions creates a significant privilege escalation risk.

Attackers could exploit publicly accessible Functions lacking authentication, gaining unauthorized access. Risky permissions, such as 'Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory/b2cDirectories/write' and 'Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write', then allow escalation to perform actions like modifying Azure AD or accessing sensitive secrets. This compromises the entire cloud environment.

Mitigate this by immediately enforcing authentication for all Azure Functions. Review and restrict permissions granted to the Function App, ensuring only necessary privileges are assigned. This principle of least privilege minimizes the impact of potential breaches.

Disable public access to the Azure Function App. Implement and regularly review a least privilege access policy. This prevents unauthorized access and limits the potential damage from any compromise.

column1: Remote Code Execution (RCE) risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable Azure Function [Node.js, CVE-2021-21315]
column3:
Publicly accessible Azure Functions using vulnerable Node.js (CVE-2021-21315) create a significant Remote Code Execution (RCE) risk. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to execute arbitrary commands on the underlying system.

Attackers may leverage the public exposure of the Azure Function to inject malicious commands through vulnerable parameters. Successful exploitation grants the attacker complete control over the function's host, potentially leading to data breaches, system compromise, and further lateral movement within the cloud environment.

Mitigation involves immediately patching the Node.js vulnerability (CVE-2021-21315) in the affected Azure Function. Restricting network access to the function, using appropriate authentication and authorization mechanisms, and implementing robust input validation are crucial best practices to prevent future exploitation.

To prevent future occurrences, enforce least privilege 'access control' policies, regularly scan for vulnerabilities, and promptly apply security updates. Immediately remediate the identified vulnerability and restrict public access to the Azure Function.

column1: Azure Resource Group does not have a resource lock
column3:
Azure Resource Manager locks provide a way to lock down Azure resources from being deleted or modified. The lock level can be set to either 'CanNotDelete' or 'ReadOnly'. When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within the scope inherit the same lock, and the most restrictive lock takes precedence.

This policy identifies Azure Resource Groups that do not have a lock set. As a best practice, place a lock on important resources to prevent accidental or malicious modification or deletion by unauthorized users.

column1: HTTP request smuggling risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instance [HAProxy, CVE-2023-25725]
column3:
Publicly exposed AWS EC2 instances running vulnerable HAProxy (CVE-2023-25725) pose a significant HTTP request smuggling risk. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to inject malicious requests, bypassing security controls and potentially gaining unauthorized access.

Attackers might leverage this vulnerability by crafting specially formatted HTTP requests. These requests can be used to manipulate the application's state, potentially leading to data breaches, server-side request forgery, or session hijacking. The public exposure of the EC2 instance significantly increases the attack surface and ease of exploitation.

Mitigation involves updating HAProxy to a patched version that addresses CVE-2023-25725. This ensures the vulnerability is remediated, preventing attackers from exploiting the flaw. Additionally, ensure the EC2 instance is not publicly accessible unless absolutely necessary, restricting access through appropriate security groups and network configurations.

Immediately patch HAProxy to the latest version. Restrict network access to the EC2 instance using security groups, allowing only necessary inbound traffic. Regularly scan for vulnerabilities and maintain up-to-date software.

column3:
GCP Virtual Machines with vulnerable Drupal installations (CVE-2018-7600) are susceptible to Remote Code Execution (RCE) attacks via Drupalgeddon2 exploits.

Attackers could exploit this attack path by leveraging publicly available exploits targeting the known vulnerability in Drupal. Successful exploitation grants attackers complete control over the compromised Virtual Machine, potentially leading to data breaches, system compromise, and further lateral movement within the cloud environment.

Mitigation involves immediately updating the vulnerable Drupal installation to a patched version. This eliminates the vulnerability, removing the attack path. Prioritize patching based on a risk assessment and prioritize critical systems.

To avoid future exploitation, implement a robust patching strategy for all software components. Regular vulnerability scanning and automated patching processes are crucial.

column1: Privilege escalation risk due to a publicly exposed and vulnerable GCP VM instance with Cloud Function Creation permissions
column3:
Publicly exposed and vulnerable Google Compute Engine (GCE) VMs with 'cloudfunctions.functions.create', 'cloudfunctions.functions.sourceCodeSet', and 'iam.serviceAccounts.actAs' permissions pose a significant privilege escalation risk.

Attackers exploiting a vulnerability on a publicly accessible GCE VM could gain initial access. With 'cloudfunctions.functions.create' and 'cloudfunctions.functions.sourceCodeSet', they can deploy malicious Cloud Functions. 'iam.serviceAccounts.actAs' allows impersonation of service accounts, enabling further privilege escalation and potentially compromising sensitive data or resources.

Mitigation involves immediately patching vulnerabilities on the GCE VM. Restrict network access to only necessary IP addresses or VPC networks. Revoke unnecessary permissions, following the principle of least privilege; ensure only required permissions are granted for the affected service accounts.

To prevent future issues, regularly scan for vulnerabilities. Implement robust network security controls, and enforce strong access control policies. Regularly review and audit service account permissions.

column1: Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF) risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS Lambda function [Node.js, CVE-2020-28168]
column3:
Publicly accessible AWS Lambda functions written in Node.js and vulnerable to CVE-2020-28168 pose a significant Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) risk. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to make the Lambda function issue HTTP requests to arbitrary domains, potentially accessing internal systems or exfiltrating sensitive data.

Attackers might leverage this vulnerability by crafting malicious requests to the exposed Lambda function. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to perform actions such as accessing internal resources, performing unauthorized data retrieval, or launching further attacks against other systems. This compromises the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the targeted resources.

Mitigation involves updating the Node.js runtime environment to a patched version that addresses CVE-2020-28168. Restricting access to the Lambda function by configuring appropriate IAM permissions, such as limiting the 'lambda:InvokeFunction' permission to authorized principals only, is crucial. Regular security patching and vulnerability scanning are essential best practices.

Immediately update the Node.js runtime to the patched version. Enforce least privilege access control for the Lambda function by restricting the 'lambda:InvokeFunction' permission to only authorized entities. Implement robust input validation and sanitization to prevent malicious requests from being processed.

It is recommended to use private IPv4 addresses for communication between EC2 instances and disassociate the public IP address from an instance or disable auto-assign public IP addresses in the subnet.

column3: Outside collaborators are not explicit members of the GitHub organization, and are usually used to allow contributors from outside the company (as contractors) to collaborate on specific repositories. column1: Azure Storage Account storing Cognitive service diagnostic logs is publicly accessible
column3:
Publicly accessible Azure Storage Accounts storing Cognitive service diagnostic logs present a significant security risk. These logs may contain sensitive information, including platform, resource, trace, and metric data, potentially providing attackers with details to carry out malicious activities.

Azure Storage Accounts are used to store Cognitive service diagnostic logs. If improperly configured with public access, attackers can easily retrieve this sensitive log data. This access could enable attackers to understand system architecture, identify vulnerabilities, and subsequently compromise the system.

Compromise of diagnostic logs could lead to data breaches, service disruptions, and significant reputational damage. Restricting access to only authorized services ensures that sensitive data remains protected and limits the potential impact of a breach.

Mitigate this risk by configuring your Azure Storage Accounts to only allow access from trusted IP addresses or specific services. Regularly review and update access control lists to maintain a strong security posture and minimize your attack surface.

column1: GCP Users and Machine Identities with IAM Data Read permissions are unused for 90 days
column3:
This policy identifies GCP identities with Unused Data Write Permissions.

Even seemingly innocuous permissions like "Data Read" in GCP IAM can be risky if left unused for extended periods. Unused GCP users and machine identities with Data Read permissions for 90 days present a security concern because:
Information Gathering Tool: An attacker wielding such credentials could use them to gather sensitive details about your GCP environment. This information could include project structures, storage buckets, or virtual machine configurations. Attackers could exploit this knowledge to identify vulnerabilities or plan more targeted attacks.
Potential Stepping Stone: A compromised unused user with Data Read permissions could be a stepping stone for attackers. They might leverage this access to discover and exploit further vulnerabilities within your GCP project, potentially leading to unauthorized access to more sensitive data or systems.

Mitigating the Risk:
Regular Review and Removal: Regularly identify and remove unused GCP user accounts and machine identities with any level of IAM Data Read permissions (Read or Write) on a scheduled basis.
Principle of Least Privilege: Always adhere to the principle of least privilege. Grant only the minimum level of Data Read access required for a user or machine identity to function ly. Evaluate if alternative methods, like IAM conditions, can restrict access to specific resources or data sets.
Monitor for Suspicious Activity: Utilize Stackdriver Logging to track activity logs, including access attempts for GCP user accounts and service accounts. This can help detect unusual activity related to unused accounts that might indicate a compromise.

column1: Cloud Log tampering risk due to a publicly exposed and vulnerable GCP VM instance with permissions to disrupt logging
column3:
Compromised publicly exposed GCP VMs with 'logging.logMetrics.delete', 'logging.logMetrics.update', 'logging.buckets.delete', 'logging.buckets.update', 'logging.logs.delete', 'logging.sinks.delete', and 'logging.sinks.update' permissions pose a significant security risk. Malicious actors could exploit vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access.

Attackers might exploit known vulnerabilities on a publicly accessible VM. Successful exploitation grants access, potentially allowing modification or deletion of log data via the assigned permissions. This compromises audit trails and hinders investigation capabilities. Data loss and inability to trace malicious activities are major consequences.

Mitigation involves restricting public access to the VM instance. Immediately revoke or restrict the excessive logging permissions granted to the VM. Implement least privilege access control, granting only necessary permissions. Regular vulnerability scanning and patching are crucial to prevent exploitation.

To prevent future occurrences, enforce least privilege, regularly review and adjust permissions assigned to VMs. Implement strong network security controls, such as firewalls, to prevent unauthorized access. Prioritize patching known vulnerabilities promptly.

column1: Encryption algorithm not using secure modes and padding

For block cipher encryption algorithms, avoid using the ECB mode as it doesn't provide serious message confidentiality. Avoid using CBC with padding due to vulnerability to padding oracle attacks. Use modes like GCM, CCM, CWC, EAX, IAPM, and OCB, as they are designed to provide both data authenticity and confidentiality. For RSA encryption, use the OAEP padding scheme.

column1: Remote code execution risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instance [ClamAV, CVE-2023-20032]
column3:
Publicly accessible AWS EC2 instances with the ClamAV vulnerability (CVE-2023-20032) pose a significant remote code execution risk. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and control of the instance.

Exploitation could involve scanning for publicly exposed instances, identifying the vulnerability, and executing malicious code. This allows attackers 'read' and 'write' access to sensitive data, potentially leading to data breaches, service disruption, or further lateral movement within the organization's infrastructure.

Mitigation involves immediately patching the ClamAV vulnerability on the affected EC2 instance using the latest available updates. Restricting network access to the EC2 instance by configuring appropriate security group rules is also critical, limiting access only to necessary internal and external sources.

To prevent future occurrences, regularly update all software on EC2 instances, employ automated vulnerability scanning, and implement robust security group configurations. Immediately patch the identified vulnerability and restrict network access to the affected instance.

column1: Roles with high privileges can be assumed by a service in an external account

An external account is one not known to Prisma cloud as part of your organization and not that of a known vendor. This policy relies on the default account group, therefore if the group is changed this policy will not reflect the environment entirely. The default account group is created upon onboarding to Prisma Cloud, and contains all instance-related accounts known to Prisma Cloud. External accounts are considered as such if Prisma are unaware of them in the context of your environment (i.e not part of the onboarded accounts). As we do not have visibility or control over the external entity, giving it the ability to gain administartive permissions in the environment is considered high risk.

column1: Privilege escalation risk due to sensitive information detected in server response on GCP VM instance with privilege escalation permissions
column3:
Unsecured GCP VM instances with excessive permissions expose sensitive data in server responses, enabling privilege escalation. Attackers might exploit vulnerabilities to gain access, retrieve sensitive credentials from server responses, and leverage elevated permissions ('accessapproval.requests.approve', 'iam.serviceAccounts.create', etc.) to compromise the entire system.

Malicious actors could craft requests to extract sensitive information, such as API keys or database credentials, from the VM's responses. These credentials, coupled with inappropriately granted permissions, facilitate unauthorized access and control, leading to data breaches, resource hijacking, and potential lateral movement within the cloud environment.

Mitigate this risk by implementing robust input validation and output sanitization to prevent sensitive data exposure in server responses. Enforce the principle of least privilege; assign only necessary permissions to VM instances. Regularly review and revoke unnecessary access rights to reduce the attack surface.

Immediately review and restrict server responses to prevent sensitive data leakage. Implement strong access controls and regularly audit IAM permissions. Adopt a least-privilege model, granting only the minimum permissions required for each VM instance.

column1: Privilege escalation risk due to a publicly exposed unauthenticated AWS Lambda function with iam:PassRole and Redshift Cluster Creation permissions
column3:
Unauthenticated AWS Lambda functions with 'iam:PassRole' and 'redshift:CreateCluster' permissions pose a significant privilege escalation risk. Malicious actors can exploit this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and create Redshift clusters.

Attackers could leverage a publicly accessible Lambda function lacking authentication. By exploiting this, they can assume the role associated with the Lambda function, potentially gaining access to sensitive data and resources within the Redshift cluster. This allows escalation to higher privileges, facilitating further malicious activity.

Mitigate this risk by configuring Lambda function authentication to 'AWS_IAM'. This ensures only authorized users with appropriate IAM roles can invoke the function. Implement the principle of least privilege, granting only necessary permissions to the Lambda function's execution role. Regularly review and revoke unnecessary permissions.

Immediately remove public access to the Lambda function. Configure appropriate authentication and authorization mechanisms. Adopt least privilege practices for all IAM roles associated with Lambda functions and other AWS services.

A network security group contains a list of security rules that allow or deny inbound or outbound network traffic based on source or destination IP address, port, and protocol. column1: AI model theft risk due to publicly exposed Storage Bucket containing GCP Vertex AI model
column3:
Publicly exposed GCP storage buckets containing GCP Vertex AI models pose a significant risk of intellectual property theft and data breaches. Unauthorized access to these buckets exposes sensitive model artifacts, potentially leading to the misuse or replication of valuable AI models.

Attackers could exploit this attack path by directly accessing the publicly exposed storage bucket. This exposes the AI model to download, analysis, and replication, resulting in the loss of competitive advantage and potential financial damage. Compromised models may also be used maliciously.

Mitigate this risk by implementing robust access controls. Restrict bucket access to only authorized users and services using appropriate Identity and Access Management ('IAM') roles. Regularly review and audit bucket permissions to ensure adherence to the principle of least privilege.

Immediately remediate by setting appropriate access controls on the storage bucket. Adopt a least privilege approach, granting only necessary permissions to authorized entities. Regularly scan for publicly accessible storage buckets and enforce strong access control policies for all storage resources.

column1: Remote code execution risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable GCP VM instance (Microsoft Message Queuing (MSMQ), CVE-2023-21554)
column3:
Publicly exposed GCP VMs with the vulnerable Microsoft Message Queuing (MSMQ) service (CVE-2023-21554) risk remote code execution. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to compromise the system.

Attackers may scan for publicly accessible VMs running MSMQ. Successful exploitation of CVE-2023-21554 grants attackers arbitrary code execution on the host, potentially leading to data breaches, privilege escalation, and further lateral movement within the cloud environment. This poses significant risks to data confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Mitigate this risk by immediately patching the MSMQ service with the relevant security update to address CVE-2023-21554. Restrict network access to the VM instance using appropriate firewall rules, ensuring only authorized traffic can reach it. This minimizes the attack surface and prevents unauthorized access.

To prevent future occurrences, regularly update all software components on VMs. Implement a robust vulnerability management program, including automated patching and regular security scans. Restrict public access to only necessary services.

column1: Azure storage account infrastructure encryption is disabled
column3:
The policy identifies Azure storage accounts for which infrastructure encryption is disabled.

Infrastructure double encryption adds a second layer of encryption using service-managed keys. When infrastructure encryption is enabled for a storage account or an encryption scope, data is encrypted twice. Once at the service level and once at the infrastructure level - with two different encryption algorithms and two different keys. It is recommended to restrict CIFS port 445 access to only trusted networks to prevent unauthorized access and data breaches.

column1: GCP AlloyDB Instance with insecure password policy
column3:
Insecure password policies on GCP AlloyDB instances allow unauthorized access. Weak or easily guessable passwords increase the risk of database compromise.

GCP AlloyDB instances utilize password-based authentication. A weak password policy increases the likelihood of brute-force or credential stuffing attacks leading to data breaches and unauthorized modifications. Failure to enforce strong passwords exposes the database to significant security risks.

Compromised AlloyDB instances can result in data exfiltration, service disruption, and financial losses. Enforcing a robust password policy significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized access by requiring complex and regularly updated passwords.

Implement a strong password policy for all AlloyDB instances. Ensure 'password.enforce_complexity', 'password.enforce_expiration', and 'password.enforce_password_does_not_contain_username' are set to 'on'. 'password.expiration_in_days' should be less than 90, 'password.min_pass_length' greater than or equal to 10, and 'password.min_uppercase_letters' and 'password.min_numerical_chars' should be at least 1. Regularly review and update password policies.

column1: Remote code execution risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instance [Apache, CVE-2022-42889]
column3:
Publicly accessible AWS EC2 instances with the Apache vulnerability CVE-2022-42889 allow attackers to execute arbitrary code.

Attackers can exploit this vulnerability by sending malicious requests to the exposed instance. Successful exploitation grants complete control, leading to data breaches, service disruptions, or further lateral movement within the environment. This risk is heightened by the public accessibility of the EC2 instance, removing a significant layer of initial protection.

Mitigation involves patching the affected Apache instances with the appropriate security updates. This addresses the root cause of the vulnerability, preventing attackers from exploiting the known weakness. Regular security patching and vulnerability scanning are essential best practices for maintaining a secure cloud environment.

Immediately patch the vulnerable Apache instances with the latest security updates. Implement robust security monitoring and intrusion detection to identify and respond to potential exploitation attempts. Regularly scan for vulnerabilities and enforce least privilege access controls.

column1: Remote code execution (RCE) exploitation attempt on AWS EC2 instance with known exploitable vulnerability [Log4j, CVE-2021-44228]
column3:
Unauthorized remote code execution attempts targeting AWS EC2 instances with the Log4j vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) pose a significant security risk. Attackers exploit this vulnerability by sending malicious requests containing specially crafted strings that trigger code execution on the vulnerable server. Successful exploitation grants attackers complete control, leading to data breaches, system compromise, and further lateral movement within the environment.

Mitigation involves patching the vulnerable Log4j instances to the latest version. This eliminates the vulnerability's exploitability, preventing attackers from leveraging it for remote code execution. Prioritize patching and actively monitor for any unusual network activity or suspicious processes on affected EC2 instances. Regular security scans are crucial for identifying vulnerable systems.

To prevent future exploitation, implement a robust vulnerability management program. Regularly update and patch all software components, especially those with known vulnerabilities. Employ web application firewalls (WAFs) to filter malicious traffic and intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS) to monitor network traffic for suspicious patterns.

Immediately patch the vulnerable Log4j instances. Enable enhanced logging and monitoring to detect any further attempts at exploitation. Implement a regular patching schedule and rigorous vulnerability scanning to proactively identify and remediate weaknesses.

For example, a workflow that prints the title of new GitHub issues to the standard output stream, would allow an attacker to create a GitHub issue with a malicious title that would be evaluated by the workflow. column1: AWS ECS task definition is not configured with read-only access to container root filesystems
column3:
This policy identifies the AWS Elastic Container Service (ECS) task definitions with readonlyRootFilesystem parameter set to false or if the parameter does not exist in the container definition within the task definition.

ECS root filesystem is the base filesystem that containers run on, providing the necessary environment and isolation for the containerized application.
If a containerized application is compromised, it could enable an attacker to alter the root file system of the host machine, thus compromising the entire system or application. This could lead to significant data loss, system crashes, or a broader security breach. 

It is recommended to limit all ECS containers to have read-only access on ECS task definition to limit the potential impact of a compromised container.

column1: AWS Network ACLs allow ingress traffic on Admin ports 22/3389
column3:
This policy identifies the AWS Network Access Control List (NACL) which has a rule to allow ingress traffic to server administration ports.

AWS NACL provides filtering of ingress and egress network traffic to AWS resources. Allowing ingress traffic on admin ports 22 (SSH) and 3389 (RDP) via AWS Network ACLs increases the vulnerability of EC2 instances and other network resources to unauthorized access and cyberattacks.

It is recommended that no NACL allows unrestricted ingress access to server administration ports, such as SSH port 22 and RDP port 3389.

NOTE: This policy may report NACLs, which include the deny policy in the rule set. Make sure while remediating the rule set does not consist of the Allow and Deny rule set together; which leads to overlap on each ruleset.

column1: Denial of Service (DoS) risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable GCP Cloud Function [Python, CVE-2021-20270]
column3:
Publicly exposed GCP Cloud Functions written in Python and vulnerable to CVE-2021-20270 pose a significant Denial of Service (DoS) risk. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to render the function unavailable, impacting service availability.

Malicious actors could leverage the public exposure to send crafted requests exploiting the CVE-2021-20270 vulnerability. This could lead to resource exhaustion and a denial-of-service condition, disrupting application functionality and potentially impacting business operations.

Mitigation involves patching the vulnerability by updating the Cloud Function's runtime environment to a version that addresses CVE-2021-20270. Restricting network access to the Cloud Function, using 'setIamPolicy' to grant only necessary permissions, is crucial to prevent unauthorized access.

Immediately patch the Cloud Function to address CVE-2021-20270. Restrict access to the function by configuring appropriate IAM roles and network firewall rules, limiting access to authorized internal networks only.

column1: AWS Web Application Firewall v2 (AWS WAFv2) logging is disabled
column3:
This policy identifies Web Application Firewall v2s (AWS WAFv2) for which logging is disabled. Enabling WAFv2 logging, logs all web requests inspected by the service which can be used for debugging and additional forensics. The logs will help to understand why certain rules are triggered and why certain web requests are blocked. You can also integrate the logs with any SIEM and log analysis tools for further analysis. It is recommended to enable logging on your Web Application Firewall v2s (WAFv2).

For details:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/logging.html#logging-management

NOTE: Global (CloudFront) WAFv2 resources are out of scope for this policy.

column1: Remote code execution (RCE) exploitation attempt on Azure Virtual Machine with known exploitable vulnerability [WebLogic, CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2019-2729]
column3:
Azure Virtual Machines running vulnerable WebLogic versions (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2019-2729) are susceptible to remote code execution (RCE) attacks. Attackers exploit these vulnerabilities by sending malicious requests to the WebLogic server, potentially gaining unauthorized access and control of the affected VM. This compromises data confidentiality, integrity, and availability, leading to significant security risks.

Successful exploitation allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on the compromised VM. They can then steal sensitive data, install malware, launch further attacks against other systems within the network, or disrupt services. The impact ranges from data breaches and financial losses to reputational damage and regulatory fines.

Mitigation involves promptly patching the vulnerable WebLogic instances with the latest security updates. Regularly scanning for vulnerabilities and updating software are crucial best practices. Implementing robust network segmentation and intrusion detection/prevention systems can further reduce the attack surface and enhance early detection capabilities.

Immediately patch the vulnerable WebLogic servers to the latest version. Enable strong authentication and authorization mechanisms, regularly update software, and conduct penetration testing to identify and address other potential vulnerabilities. Implementing a centralized vulnerability management system is strongly recommended.

column1: Remote code execution (RCE) exploitation attempt on GCP VM with known exploitable vulnerability [Log4j, CVE-2021-44228]
column3:
Unauthorized remote code execution attempts targeting Google Cloud Platform (GCP) virtual machines (VMs) with the known Log4j vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) pose a significant security risk. Attackers could leverage this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and control of the affected VMs. Successful exploitation could lead to data breaches, service disruptions, and further compromise of the cloud environment.

Malicious actors may exploit the Log4j vulnerability by sending specially crafted network requests to the vulnerable GCP VM. These requests trigger the vulnerability, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary code on the VM with the privileges of the affected application or service. This grants the attacker significant control, potentially leading to data exfiltration, system manipulation, or lateral movement within the cloud environment.

Mitigation requires immediate patching of the vulnerable Log4j instances on all affected GCP VMs. This involves upgrading to a patched version of the Log4j library that addresses the CVE-2021-44228 vulnerability. Regular vulnerability scanning and patching should be implemented as a best practice to prevent future exploitation attempts.

To prevent future exploitation, prioritize timely patching of all software components. Implement robust vulnerability management processes, including regular security scanning and automated patching. Enable 'Cloud Logging' and 'Cloud Audit Logging' for enhanced monitoring and threat detection capabilities.

column1: AWS ElastiCache Redis cluster is not configured with automatic backup
column3:
This policy identifies Amazon ElastiCache Redis clusters where automatic backup is disabled by checking if SnapshotRetentionLimit is less than 1.

Amazon ElastiCache for Redis clusters can back up their data. Automatic backups in ElastiCache Redis clusters ensure data durability and enable point-in-time recovery, protecting against data loss or corruption. Without backups, data loss from breaches or corruption could be irreversible, compromising data integrity and availability.

It is recommended to enable automatic backups to adhere to compliance requirements and enhance security measures, ensuring data integrity and resilience against potential threats.

column1: Remote code execution risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable Azure Virtual Machine [Linux Kernel, CVE-2022-47939]
column3:
Publicly accessible Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) with the Linux kernel vulnerability CVE-2022-47939 are susceptible to remote code execution. This poses a significant risk of unauthorized access, data breaches, and system compromise.

Attackers can exploit this vulnerability by sending malicious network traffic to the exposed VM. Successful exploitation grants them complete control, potentially enabling data exfiltration, malware deployment, or further lateral movement within the organization's infrastructure. The public exposure significantly increases the attack surface and ease of compromise.

Mitigation involves immediately patching the vulnerable Linux kernel with the appropriate security update. This eliminates the vulnerability and prevents attackers from exploiting the flaw. Regular security patching and vulnerability scanning are crucial best practices.

Restrict network access to the VM, using Network Security Groups or similar mechanisms, to limit exposure only to necessary sources. Immediately apply the kernel patch and verify its successful deployment to prevent exploitation. Regularly update the VM's operating system and applications.

column1: Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploitation attempt on AWS EC2 instance with known exploitable vulnerability [OctoberCMS, CVE-2021-32648]
column3:
Unauthorized remote code execution (RCE) attempts targeting AWS EC2 instances with the known OctoberCMS vulnerability (CVE-2021-32648) pose a significant security risk. Attackers could leverage this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and control of affected EC2 instances. Successful exploitation could lead to data breaches, system compromise, and disruption of services.

Exploitation typically involves an attacker sending malicious requests exploiting the vulnerability in OctoberCMS. This could be achieved through various attack vectors, such as web requests or crafted network traffic. The success of the attack depends on the attacker's knowledge of the vulnerability and the security posture of the affected EC2 instance. Compromised systems may be used for further malicious activities, like launching attacks against other systems.

Mitigation involves promptly patching the vulnerable OctoberCMS application on all affected EC2 instances. Updating to a version that addresses CVE-2021-32648 eliminates the vulnerability, preventing exploitation. Regular patching and vulnerability scanning are crucial best practices to minimize this risk. Implementing robust intrusion detection and prevention systems also provides an additional layer of security.

To prevent future occurrences, immediately update OctoberCMS to a patched version. Implement a rigorous patching schedule and integrate automated vulnerability scanning into your security workflows. Regularly review and update security configurations for your AWS EC2 instances.

Mitigate this risk by immediately removing unnecessary IAM permissions from the EC2 instance roles. Apply the principle of least privilege, granting only the permissions absolutely required for the instance's function. Regularly review and update IAM permissions to reflect changing needs.

Restrict public access to EC2 instances. Implement robust security measures such as network segmentation, intrusion detection, and vulnerability scanning. Patch all known vulnerabilities promptly to prevent exploitation.

column1: Privilege escalation risk due to Shellshock payload detected on traffic targetting a vulnerable GCP VM instance with privilege escalation permissions
column3:
Unsecured GCP VMs with Shellshock vulnerability and excessive permissions pose a significant privilege escalation risk. Attackers can exploit the Shellshock vulnerability (CVE-2014-6271) in traffic targeting vulnerable VMs to execute arbitrary code. This, coupled with excessive permissions like 'iam.serviceAccounts.create' or 'compute.instances.setIamPolicy', allows attackers to gain unauthorized access and control of the system.

The attack involves malicious actors sending crafted HTTP requests exploiting the Shellshock vulnerability to a vulnerable GCP VM. Successful exploitation allows execution of arbitrary code. If the VM possesses permissions such as 'iam.serviceAccounts.create' or 'compute.instances.setIamPolicy', the attacker can elevate privileges, potentially compromising the entire GCP environment.

Mitigation involves promptly patching the vulnerable Bash version on the affected VMs to address the Shellshock vulnerability. Immediately revoke unnecessary permissions assigned to the VM. Implement robust network security measures, like Web Application Access Security (WAAS) rules, to filter malicious traffic.

To prevent future occurrences, enforce a strict least-privilege policy for all VMs. Regularly scan for and remediate vulnerabilities. Implement intrusion detection and prevention systems, coupled with rigorous security monitoring to quickly identify and respond to suspicious activities.

column1: AWS S3 bucket publicly writable
column3:
Publicly writable AWS S3 buckets allow unauthorized access to sensitive data stored within. This misconfiguration exposes data to malicious actors and data breaches.

The S3 service relies on Access Control Lists (ACLs) and bucket policies to manage access. Incorrectly configured ACLs or bucket policies that grant 'Put', 'Create','Update', 'Replicate', 'Write', or 'Delete' permissions to the world, allow anyone to modify or delete bucket contents. This exposes data to unauthorized access, modification, or deletion.

A successful attack could lead to data exfiltration, modification, or deletion, resulting in significant financial, legal, and reputational damage. Best practices dictate strict control over S3 bucket permissions to prevent unauthorized access. Data loss and compliance violations are possible consequences.

Implement least privilege access controls. Restrict access to only trusted users and services via appropriately configured ACLs and bucket policies. Regularly review and audit S3 bucket permissions to identify and rectify any misconfigurations. Use strong encryption to protect data at rest and in transit. Employ multi-factor authentication (MFA) for enhanced security.

Note: This policy excludes AWS S3 buckets that are configured to host public static websites.

This policy identifies GCP Vertex AI Workbench instances with Secure Boot disabled.

Secure Boot is a security feature that ensures only trusted, digitally signed software runs during the boot process, protecting against advanced threats such as rootkits and bootkits. By verifying the integrity of the bootloader and operating system, Secure Boot prevents unauthorized software from compromising the system at startup. Without Secure Boot, instances are vulnerable to persistent malware and unauthorized code that could compromise the system deeply.

It is recommended to enable Secure Boot for Vertex AI Workbench instances.

column1: Azure Storage Account default network access is set to 'Allow'
column3:
Azure Storage accounts with default network access set to 'Allow' are susceptible to unauthorized data access. This misconfiguration exposes storage account resources to any network, increasing the risk of data breaches and unauthorized modifications.

Azure Storage accounts offer a 'Network rules' setting to control inbound traffic. By default, 'Allow' grants access from any IP address. Untrusted IPs can exploit this, leading to data exfiltration, ransomware attacks, or malicious data manipulation. Restricting network access enhances security posture significantly.

The impact of this misconfiguration includes data breaches, unauthorized resource modification, and potential compliance violations. Implementing strong access controls through network rules is crucial to protect sensitive data and maintain regulatory compliance. Restricting access to only authorized networks minimizes the attack surface.

To mitigate this risk, configure your Azure Storage accounts to explicitly allow access only from trusted IP addresses or virtual networks. Utilize the 'Network rules' setting within the storage account configuration to define specific allowed networks. Regularly review and update these rules as your infrastructure evolves.

column1: Remote code execution (RCE) risk due to a publicly exposed AWS EC2 instance with Spring4Shell vulnerability
column3:
Publicly accessible AWS EC2 instances with the Spring4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2022-22965 and CVE-2022-22963) pose a significant risk of remote code execution (RCE).

Attackers can exploit this vulnerability through the web server, compromising applications on the affected EC2 instance. Successful exploitation allows attackers to execute arbitrary code, leading to data breaches, system control, and service disruption. Public exposure significantly increases the attack surface and ease of compromise.

Mitigation involves patching the Spring4Shell vulnerability by updating the Spring framework. Restricting network access to the EC2 instance using security groups, only allowing necessary traffic, is crucial. Regular vulnerability scanning and penetration testing are also essential.

Immediately patch the Spring framework to address the vulnerability. Implement security groups to restrict inbound traffic to only trusted sources. Prioritize continuous monitoring and proactive vulnerability management to prevent future exploitation.

column1: Remote code execution risk due to publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instance (Apache Submarine, CVE-2023-46302)
column3:
Publicly accessible AWS EC2 instances with the Apache Submarine vulnerability (CVE-2023-46302) pose a significant remote code execution risk. Attackers can exploit this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access and control of the affected system.

Compromise occurs when an attacker scans for and identifies publicly exposed EC2 instances running vulnerable Apache Submarine software. Successful exploitation grants the attacker complete control, enabling data exfiltration, privilege escalation, and further lateral movement within the cloud environment. This significantly increases the risk of data breaches and operational disruptions.

Mitigation involves immediately patching the vulnerable Apache Submarine instances with the necessary security updates. Restricting network access to only authorized IP addresses and implementing robust intrusion detection systems also reduces the attack surface. Regular security assessments and vulnerability scanning are crucial preventative measures.

To prevent future occurrences, enforce least privilege permissions, regularly update software, and utilize security groups to limit network access to essential ports. Proactive vulnerability scanning and patching are vital to maintaining a secure cloud environment.

column1: Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploitation attempt on AWS EC2 instance with known exploitable vulnerability [Nginx PHP-FPM, CVE-2019-11043]
column3:
Remote code execution (RCE) attempts targeting AWS EC2 instances with the known vulnerable Nginx PHP-FPM [CVE-2019-11043] are detected.

Attackers could exploit this attack path by leveraging publicly known exploits targeting the vulnerable Nginx PHP-FPM version installed on the EC2 instance. Successful exploitation grants attackers complete control, leading to data breaches, system compromise, and potential lateral movement within the infrastructure.

Mitigation involves immediately updating the Nginx PHP-FPM software to a patched version addressing CVE-2019-11043. This eliminates the vulnerability, preventing attackers from exploiting this attack path. Regular patching and vulnerability scanning are crucial for proactive security.

To avoid future exploitation, enforce a rigorous patching schedule for all software components on EC2 instances. Implement a vulnerability scanner to proactively identify and remediate vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. Regular security audits are recommended.

column1: Potentially unauthorized malware activity detected via traffic to suspicious domains on a publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instance
column3:
Publicly exposed and vulnerable AWS EC2 instances communicating with suspicious domains indicate potential malware activity. Unauthorized access could compromise confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Attackers exploit known vulnerabilities on these exposed instances to gain unauthorized access. They then use the compromised machine to communicate with command-and-control servers, often using suspicious domains associated with malware distribution or malicious activities like cryptomining. This leads to data breaches, system disruptions, and increased operational costs.

Mitigate this risk by immediately patching known vulnerabilities on EC2 instances. Restrict public access to these instances using security groups, only allowing necessary inbound traffic. Regularly scan for vulnerabilities and implement robust intrusion detection systems.

Implement a security information and event management (SIEM) system to monitor network traffic for connections to suspicious domains. Enforce strong 'iam:PasswordPolicy' to improve password security, and promptly investigate any alerts indicating communication with malicious domains. Isolate affected instances immediately.

column1: AWS S3 Buckets Block public access bucket policy setting disabled
column3:
AWS S3 buckets with the 'Block public access' setting disabled or 'Block public access to buckets and objects granted through new public bucket or access point policies' setting or 'Block public and cross-account access to buckets and objects through any public bucket or access point policies' disabled pose a significant security risk, allowing unauthorized access to sensitive data.

The 'Block public access' setting in Amazon S3 controls public accessibility of buckets and objects. Disabling this setting, either intentionally or through misconfiguration, exposes data to the internet, potentially leading to data breaches, unauthorized modification, or ransomware attacks by malicious actors or accidental exposure.

The impact of this misconfiguration can range from data loss and regulatory non-compliance to reputational damage and financial losses. Enabling this setting ensures only authorized users can access the data, minimizing the risk of data breaches and improving overall security posture.

To mitigate this risk, enable the 'Block all public access' setting for all S3 buckets. Alternatively, use 'Block public access to buckets and objects granted through new public bucket or access point policies' and 'Block public and cross-account access to buckets and objects through any public bucket or access point policies', depending on your specific requirements. Regularly review and audit S3 bucket configurations to prevent accidental or malicious changes.
